title.en: Rudra asked to spare our people and to come with his weapon laid aside

summary: Twelve ṛks, the first ṛks of the Namakam after the yajus of anuvākas 2–9. The worshipper asks Rudra not to frighten, harm or slay his people, his children and his cattle, offers him a prayer for the welfare of the village, asks that his weapon and ill-will pass by and his thousand weapons fall on others, and that he lay his weapon on a high tree and come wearing his hide and carrying only his bow. Sāyaṇa reads the hymn through Rudra’s two bodies, the fierce one that is to stay far away and the kindly one that heals and is to come near.

samasa.meaning: blue and red; Sāyaṇa: blue in the throat, red elsewhere

vyakarana.note: Vocative of pati. With the genitive andhasaḥ it makes the Vedic vocative phrase andhasas pate, ‘O lord of the Soma juice / of food’: the genitive keeps its s before pati (the text writes अन्धसस्पते). The padaccheda keeps the two words apart.

Present participle of daridrā, an intensive of drā ‘run’ (‘roam about; be in want’). Reduplicated stems make the participle without n (daridrat, not daridrant); the vocative is the bare stem, and its t becomes n before nīla-.

Aorist of bhī ‘fear’, without augment because of mā (na māṅyoge, P. 6.4.74). MW records the aorist 2nd sg. bhes, ‘esp. in mā bhes, do not be afraid’. Sāyaṇa glosses it with the causative, मा भीषय, and supplies समूहं, ‘the multitude’ [of these men and cattle], as its object.
Following Sāyaṇa’s division माऽरो = mā araḥ: the a-aorist of ṛ ‘go’ (MW: aor. ārat), augmentless with mā. Sāyaṇa: ‘let nothing go [to ruin]’ (मा गच्छतु … मा विनश्यतु).
mo = mā + u, ‘and … not’; the u adds ‘and’ to the prohibition, which carries on to amamat. The fused mo is pragṛhya and meets eṣām without sandhi.

Reduplicated aorist of the causative of am ‘be afflicted, sick’ (MW: Caus. āmayati, aor. āmamat), here without augment after mā (carried in mo): ‘let it not fall sick’. The junction canāmamat would read the same with āmamat.

translation.literal: O Drāpi, O lord of food, O destitute one, O blue-and-red one: of these men, of these cattle — do not [cause] fear, do not [let them] go [to ruin], and let not anything of these fall sick.
translation.readable: O Drāpi, lord of food, you who own nothing, blue and red: do not frighten these our people and these our cattle, let none of them perish, and let none of them fall sick.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa notes that the second to ninth anuvākas gave yajus and that the ṛks begin here. He explains drāpi as «द्रापयति कुत्सितां गतिं प्रापयतीति द्रापिः» — he who makes [the wicked] go a wretched way — «पापिनो नरकप्रदानेन क्लेशयतीत्यर्थः», ‘he torments sinners by giving them hell’. andhas is food: «अन्धोऽन्नं तस्य पतिः पालकः», and he protects the food of his devotees. daridrat is अकिंचनः, one who has nothing, himself detached and alone, for which he cites a śruti: «एकमेवाद्वितीयं ब्रह्म नेह नानाऽस्ति किंचन». nīlalohita is «कण्ठे नीलोऽन्यत्र लोहित इति नीललोहितः». He takes mā bheḥ as माभीषय, ‘do not frighten’ the multitude of our men and cattle; mā araḥ as मा गच्छतु, ‘let not one thing among them go’, that is, perish; and the last clause as «मैव रुग्णम् अभूत्», ‘let none fall sick’.
units.reflection: The first ṛk asks for no gift. It asks only that fear, loss and sickness stay away from one’s people and animals.

flags.note: māro: the Saṃhitā can be divided mā araḥ or mā raḥ. This edition follows Sāyaṇa’s division माऽरो (mā araḥ, from ṛ ‘go’). MW records under ruj ‘break’ an aorist 2nd sg. rok for the parallel in VS; a sense ‘do not hurt’ is therefore also possible.
bheḥ is intransitive, ‘fear’ (MW: mā bhes ‘do not be afraid’). Sāyaṇa glosses it causatively, ‘do not frighten’, with the genitives eṣām puruṣāṇām … as its object; the translation follows Sāyaṇa.
amamat or āmamat: after cana the junction (canāmamat) does not show whether the augment is present. With mā the augmentless form is expected; MW cites āmamat.

vyakarana.note: viśvāha is the Taittirīya form of the Vedic adverb viśvāhā / viśvahā ‘at all times’ (MW). It is compounded here with bheṣajī: in this pāda bheṣajī has no accent of its own, while in the next (rudrasya bheṣajī) it has one, which shows a compound. Sāyaṇa’s lemma also has the two together.
tanū ‘body’, also ‘one’s own form, self’. The relative yā … tanūḥ is picked up by tayā: ‘that body … with that’.
A Vedic infinitive in -ase, a dative of purpose, from jīv: ‘for living’. Sāyaṇa takes it as जीवयितुं, ‘to make [us] live’.
Imperative 2nd sg. of mṛḍ (6th class), ‘be gracious’; Sāyaṇa: सुखय.

translation.literal: That body of yours, O Rudra, which [is] kindly — kindly, healing at all times, kindly, the healing [body] of Rudra — with that be gracious to us, for [our] living.
translation.readable: O Rudra, with that kindly body of yours, kindly and healing at all times, the kindly healing form of Rudra, be gracious to us, that we may live.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes śivā as शान्ता, ‘calm’, mṛḍa as सुखय, ‘make happy’, and jīvase as जीवयितुं, ‘to make [us] live’. The body is called kindly for two reasons: it is the remedy on all days (सर्वेष्वहःसु) for disease, poverty and the like; and, as the healer for reaching oneness with Rudra («रुद्रस्य तादात्म्यप्राप्तये»), «ज्ञानप्रदानेन जन्ममरणादिदुःखं निवारयति» — by giving knowledge it removes the sorrow of birth, death and the rest.

flags.note: viśvāhabheṣajī is taken as one compound word, on the evidence of the accent (bheṣajī unaccented in this pāda) and of both witnesses, which write it together. It may also be divided viśvāha bheṣajī, ‘healing at all times’, with the same sense.

translation.literal: This thought we bring forth to Rudra, the strong, the braided-haired, the ruler of heroes, so that there may be welfare for our two-footed [and] four-footed, [and] everything in this village [be] thriving [and] free from sickness.
translation.readable: To Rudra, the mighty, with braided hair, who rules over heroes, we offer this prayer, that our people and our cattle may be well, and all in this village thrive, free from sickness.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes mati as a mind given to worship and meditation (पूजाध्यानादिविषयां बुद्धिं), which ‘we nourish greatly’ (प्रकर्षेण पोषयामः) for Rudra. tavas is बलयुक्ताय, ‘possessed of strength’, able to do what we desire; kapardin is «जटाबन्धयुक्ताय तापसवेषायेत्यर्थः», with matted locks, in the guise of an ascetic; and kṣayadvīra is क्षीयमाणप्रतिपक्षपुरुषाय, ‘he by whom the enemy’s men are destroyed’, which he also explains as the cause that destroys sin in the form of false appearance. The two-footed are our sons and grandsons, the four-footed our cows and buffaloes; the whole village is to thrive, full of ease and free from affliction: «पुष्टं सुखपूर्णमनातुरमुपद्रवरहितं».

flags.note: kṣayadvīra: MW gives ‘ruling or governing men’ (and, for Sāyaṇa on the RV, ‘possessed of abiding heroes’). Here Sāyaṇa takes it as ‘he by whom the enemy’s men are destroyed’. The word table gives both; the translation keeps the dictionary sense.
corrections.json (N10.3, orthographic): the base witness writes अस्मिन्न् before the pañcāśat mark, the second witness a single n. Same words.

translation.literal: Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and make joy for us; to you, the ruler of heroes, we would offer worship with homage. What welfare and what health father Manu won by sacrifice, may we obtain that, O Rudra, in your guidance.
translation.readable: Be gracious to us, O Rudra, and give us joy; we would worship you, ruler of heroes, with homage. The welfare and health that father Manu won by sacrifice — may we attain them, O Rudra, under your guidance.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa divides the two requests by world: mṛḍa is «मृडयेह लोके सुखय», ‘make us happy in this world’, and mayaḥ kṛdhi is «परलोकेऽपि मयः सुखं कृधि कुरु», ‘make happiness for us in the other world too’. Here he takes kṣayadvīra as क्षपितास्मदीयपापाय, ‘to you who have destroyed our sins’, and vidhema as परिचरेम, ‘may we serve’. The father is «पिता पालको मनुः प्रजापतिः» — Manu, Prajāpati, the protector; śam is happiness and yoḥ दुःखपृथग्भावं, ‘separation from sorrow’; āyaje is ‘whatever he brought about’ («यदायजे यत्किंचित्»); and praṇīti is प्रणये स्नेहातिशये, ‘in your great affection’: may we obtain all of it there.

flags.note: āyaje: the tense and formation are not certain (the regular perfect would be īje or, as MW notes, yeje). The translation follows Sāyaṇa, who takes it as past: ‘what [Manu] won by sacrifice’.

translation.literal: Do not [harm] our great one, and not our small one; not our begetting one, and not our begotten one. Do not slay our father, and not [our] mother; do not harm, O Rudra, our dear bodies.
translation.readable: Do not harm our elders or our little ones, the young man who begets or the child yet unborn; do not slay our father or our mother; do not harm, O Rudra, our dear bodies.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa supplies mā rīriṣaḥ (मा हिंसीः, ‘do not harm’) to each of the first four: mahāntam is the old man (स्थविरं पुरुषं), arbhakam the child (बालं), ukṣantam the young man able to beget (सेचन-समर्थं युवानं पुरुषं) and ukṣitam the child in the womb (गर्भस्थं पुरुषं). Father and mother go with mā vadhīḥ, and the dear bodies again with mā rīriṣaḥ: «प्रियाश्च तनुवः शरीराणि मा रीरिषः».

translation.literal: Do not harm us in [our] offspring, in [our] son, not in our life, not in our cows, not in our horses. Do not, O Rudra, enraged, slay our men; bringing oblations, we would worship you with homage.
translation.readable: Do not harm us in our children or our sons, in our life, our cattle or our horses; do not, O Rudra, in anger slay our men. With oblations we would worship you with homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: toka is any offspring (तोकेऽपत्यमात्रे), tanaya the son in particular (विशेषतः पुत्रे); mā rīriṣaḥ is ‘do not do harm’ (हिंसां मा कुरु) and is taken with each locative. The vīras are dependants (भृत्यान्), whom Rudra is asked not to slay ‘when angered’ (क्रुद्धः सन्). haviṣmantaḥ is हविर्युक्ताः, ‘we who are provided with oblations’, and vidhema is again परिचरेम.

translation.literal: Far [be] your [fierce form], of [you] the cow-slaying and man-slaying, the ruler of heroes; let your favour be with us. And protect us, and speak for [us], O god, and then grant us shelter, [you who are] doubly strong.
translation.readable: Far from us be your form that slays cattle and men, O ruler of heroes; let your kindness be with us. Protect us, O god, speak for us, and give us shelter, you who are doubly strong.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: your fierce form (तवोग्ररूपम्) — of you who slay cattle and men and destroy dependants — «आराद् अस्तु दूरे तिष्ठतु», let it stay far away; but your form that brings happiness (सुखकरं रूपं), let it be among us (अस्मास्वस्तु). He recalls the two bodies of Rudra, «घोराऽन्या शिवाऽन्येति»: the terrible one is to go far, the kindly one to come here. adhi brūhi is to speak of us among the gods as greater than the other sacrificers (देवेषु ब्रूहि). dvibarhāḥ is द्वयोर्लोकयोर्वर्धयिता, ‘you who make [us] prosper in both worlds’, and śarma yaccha is ‘give happiness’.

translation.literal: Praise the renowned one, sitting on the chariot-seat, the young, fearsome like a wild beast, the smiter, the fierce. Being praised, O Rudra, be gracious to the singer; let your hosts strike down another than us.
translation.readable: Praise the renowned one, seated on his chariot, the young, fearsome as a wild beast, the fierce destroyer. Praised by us, O Rudra, be gracious to the one who sings to you; let your hosts strike down another, not us.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes stuhi as addressed to his own speech (हे मदीयंवचः). He reads gartasad as ‘ever dwelling in the lotus of the heart, which is like a cave’ (गर्तसदृशे हृदयपुण्डरीके सर्वदा तिष्ठन्तम्), citing a smṛti: «ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति». yuvan is नित्यतरुणम्, ‘ever young’; upahatnu and ugra describe the fierce form that destroys the whole world at the dissolution (प्रलयकाले सर्वं जगत्संहर्तुमुग्ररूपिणम्); and the beast is the lion: «भीमं मृगं न भयंकरं सिंहमिव», fierce as a lion is to tear an elephant. jaritṛ he takes not as ‘singer’ but as our body, which ages and wastes day by day (जरणशीले दिने दिने क्षीयमाणेऽस्मच्छरीरे); and the hosts are to destroy ‘our enemy, other than us’ (अस्मदन्यं वैरिणं).

flags.note: gartasad: MW ‘sitting on the seat of a war-chariot’ (garta ‘high seat, chariot-seat’); Sāyaṇa: dwelling in the cave-like lotus of the heart. The literal translation follows the dictionary; the word table gives both.
jaritre: MW jaritṛ ‘invoker, praiser’; Sāyaṇa takes it as ‘to [our] body that grows old’ (from jṝ). The translation follows the dictionary sense.

translation.literal: May the weapon of Rudra pass around us; [may] the ill-will of the impetuous, malicious one [pass] around [us]. Unstring the firm [bows] from the generous; O bountiful one, be gracious to [our] offspring [and] descendant.
translation.readable: May Rudra’s weapon pass us by, and the ill-will of the fierce one bent on harm. Unstring your firm bows, away from those who give to you; O bountiful one, be gracious to our children and their children.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: heti is the weapon, «हन्यतेऽनयेति हेतिरायुधं», and it is to leave us out on every side (परितो वर्जितान्करोतु), never to pierce us. tveṣa is ‘blazing with anger’ and aghāyu ‘he who wishes harm in the form of a blow’: «क्रोधोज्ज्वलितस्याघायोरघं पापं प्रहाररूपमिच्छतो»; and durmati is «दुर्मतिरुग्रबुद्धिः», ‘fierce intent’, which is to avoid us too. He takes sthirā with this intent — «विरोधिनाशनाय या दृढा दुर्मतिरस्ति», ‘the ill-will that is firm for destroying opponents’ — and asks that Rudra slacken it and take it away («सकाशादवतनुष्वावततामपनीतां कुरु») from the sacrificers who have food in the form of oblations (हविर्लक्षणान्नयुक्तेभ्यो यजमानेभ्यः). mīḍhvas is the showerer of desires, and «तोकायास्मत्पुत्राय तनयाय तदीयपुत्राय» — toka is our son, tanaya his son.

flags.note: sthirā is grammatically a neuter plural (‘the firm [bows]’), the object of ava … tanuṣva; Sāyaṇa takes it with durmati, ‘the firm ill-will’. The translation follows the grammar; the word table gives both.

translation.literal: O most bountiful, O most kindly one, be kindly [and] well-disposed to us. Having laid [your] weapon on the highest tree, wearing the hide, come; bearing the Pināka, come.
translation.readable: Most bountiful, most kindly one, be kind and gracious to us. Lay your weapon on the highest tree and come, wearing your hide; come carrying the Pināka.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: mīḍhuṣṭama is the greatest showerer of desires, and śivatama ‘of supremely calm nature’ (शिवतमातिशयेन शान्तस्वरूप); sumanāḥ is ‘with good will and affection’ (सौमनस्येन स्नेहेन युक्तश्च). The weapon is to be laid on a very tall tree such as a banyan or an aśvattha (वटाश्वत्थादिरूपे), «यथाऽस्माभिर्न दृश्यते», ‘so that we do not see it’; kṛttiṃ vasānaḥ is व्याघ्रचर्ममात्रं परिदधान, ‘wearing only the tiger skin’. Even as he comes he is to carry the Pināka as an ornament (भूषणार्थं), only the bow in his hand (धनुर्मात्रं हस्ते), leaving the arrows and the rest behind.
units.reflection: The weapon is not destroyed; it is hung up out of sight. What is asked for is that the power be present without being aimed.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa derives vikirida from kiri, wealth scattered in abundance before devotees: «किरावो धनानि तानि ददातीति किरिदः। विशेषेण किरिदो विकिरिदः» — he who gives such wealth in a special way. For vilohita he gives two explanations: «लौहित्यरहितः श्वेत इत्यर्थः», ‘without redness, that is, white’, supported by a meditation verse of the five-syllabled mantra that the mantra-knowers remember; or ‘especially red’, supported by one of the eight-syllabled. Bhagavas is भगवन्, ‘endowed with the six excellences’ (षड्गुणसंपन्न), for which he quotes «ऐश्वर्यस्य समग्रस्य धर्मस्य यशसः श्रियः। ज्ञानवैराग्ययोश्चैव षण्णां भग इतीरणा», and a second definition of bhagavān. The thousand weapons are to destroy ‘the opponent, other than us’ (अस्मदन्यं विरोधिनं).

flags.note: vikirida: MW records the word for the TS only, ‘according to the scholiast’ meaning ‘averting wounds’ or ‘sending off arrows’; Sāyaṇa here derives it from kiri ‘wealth’ (‘giver of scattered wealth’). The translation leaves it as a name.
vilohita: MW ‘deep-red’; Sāyaṇa offers ‘not red, white’ or ‘especially red’. The translation follows the dictionary and his second explanation.

translation.literal: Thousands, in a thousand ways, [are] the weapons in your arms. Being their master, O blessed one, make [their] mouths turned away.
translation.readable: Thousands of weapons, of a thousand kinds, are in your arms; you who are their master, O Lord, turn their points away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the weapons in Rudra’s hands are of a thousand kinds by type, «जातिभेदेन सहस्रप्रकारत्वम्» — bow, sword, trident and so on — and of each kind there are thousands. Being their master and able («त्वमीशानः समर्थः»), he is asked to turn «मुखा मुखानि शल्यानि», their mouths, the heads of the weapons, away: पराङ्मुखानि कुरु.

flags.note: corrections.json (N10.12, W2 error): the second witness reads सहस्रधाः. sahasradhā is an adverb, as Sāyaṇa’s gloss सहस्रप्रकाराः and the base witness show.
